All details gathered. Here is the complete, source-grounded report.

# File-type filtering in ripgrep 14.1.1

All five flags are defined in `crates/core/flags/defs.rs`. The type-matching engine lives in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, the built-in type list in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`, and the `--type-list` output renderer in `crates/core/main.rs`.

---

## 1. Verbatim doc text for each flag

### `-t` / `--type` (defs.rs:6763-6811)
- Value variable: `TYPE`; category: Filter.
- Short (`doc_short`, line 6782): `Only search files matching TYPE.`
- Long (`doc_long`, lines 6785-6799), verbatim (roff source):
```
This flag limits ripgrep to searching files matching \fITYPE\fP. Multiple
\flag{type} flags may be provided.
.sp
This flag supports the special value \fBall\fP, which will behave as if
\flag{type} was provided for every file type supported by ripgrep (including
any custom file types). The end result is that \fB\-\-type=all\fP causes
ripgrep to search in "whitelist" mode, where it will only search files it
recognizes via its type definitions.
.sp
Note that this flag has lower precedence than both the \flag{glob} flag and
any rules found in ignore files.
.sp
To see the list of available file types, use the \flag{type-list} flag.
```

### `-T` / `--type-not` (defs.rs:6986-7033)
- Value variable: `TYPE`; category: Filter.
- Short (line 7007): `Do not search files matching TYPE.`
- Long (lines 7010-7021), verbatim:
```
Do not search files matching \fITYPE\fP. Multiple \flag{type-not} flags may be
provided. Use the \flag{type-list} flag to list all available types.
.sp
This flag supports the special value \fBall\fP, which will behave
as if \flag{type-not} was provided for every file type supported by
ripgrep (including any custom file types). The end result is that
\fB\-\-type\-not=all\fP causes ripgrep to search in "blacklist" mode, where it
will only search files that are unrecognized by its type definitions.
.sp
To see the list of available file types, use the \flag{type-list} flag.
```

### `--type-add` (defs.rs:6837-6900)
- Value variable: `TYPESPEC`; category: Filter. (No short flag.)
- Short (line 6855): `Add a new glob for a file type.`
- Long (lines 6858-6892), verbatim:
```
This flag adds a new glob for a particular file type. Only one glob can be
added at a time. Multiple \flag{type-add} flags can be provided. Unless
\flag{type-clear} is used, globs are added to any existing globs defined inside
of ripgrep.
.sp
Note that this must be passed to every invocation of ripgrep. Type settings are
not persisted. See \fBCONFIGURATION FILES\fP for a workaround.
.sp
Example:
.sp
.EX
    rg \-\-type\-add 'foo:*.foo' -tfoo \fIPATTERN\fP
.EE
.sp
This flag can also be used to include rules from other types with the special
include directive. The include directive permits specifying one or more other
type names (separated by a comma) that have been defined and its rules will
automatically be imported into the type specified. For example, to create a
type called src that matches C++, Python and Markdown files, one can use:
.sp
.EX
    \-\-type\-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md'
.EE
.sp
Additional glob rules can still be added to the src type by using this flag
again:
.sp
.EX
    \-\-type\-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' \-\-type\-add 'src:*.foo'
.EE
.sp
Note that type names must consist only of Unicode letters or numbers.
Punctuation characters are not allowed.
```

### `--type-clear` (defs.rs:6924-6961)
- Value variable: `TYPE`; category: Filter. (No short flag.)
- Short (line 6942): `Clear globs for a file type.`
- Long (lines 6945-6952), verbatim:
```
Clear the file type globs previously defined for \fITYPE\fP. This clears any
previously defined globs for the \fITYPE\fP, but globs can be added after this
flag.
.sp
Note that this must be passed to every invocation of ripgrep. Type settings are
not persisted. See \fBCONFIGURATION FILES\fP for a workaround.
```

### `--type-list` (defs.rs:7066-7097)
- Switch (takes no value); category: OtherBehaviors. (No short flag; no negation — `assert!(v.unwrap_switch(), "--type-list has no negation")`.)
- Short (line 7081): `Show all supported file types.`
- Long (lines 7084-7089), verbatim:
```
Show all supported file types and their corresponding globs. This takes any
\flag{type-add} and \flag{type-clear} flags given into account. Each type is
printed on its own line, followed by a \fB:\fP and then a comma-delimited list
of globs for that type on the same line.
```

Note on doc syntax: these strings are roff/man source. `\fI...\fP` = italic, `\fB...\fP` = bold, `\flag{type}` is a macro that expands to a cross-reference to the named flag, `.sp` = blank line, `.EX`/`.EE` delimit an example block. The same strings feed both the man page and `--help`.

---

## 2. `--type-add` syntax

Parsed by `TypesBuilder::add_def` (types.rs:433-479). The doc comment (lines 433-441) states there are exactly two valid formats:
```
1. `{name}:{glob}`.  This defines a 'root' definition that associates the
    given name with the given glob.
2. `{name}:include:{comma-separated list of already defined names}.
    This defines an 'include' definition that associates the given name
    with the definitions of the given existing types.
Names may not include any characters that are not Unicode letters or numbers.
```

Implementation details:
- The spec is split on `:` (line 443). Exactly 2 parts → `name:glob`; exactly 3 parts → the middle part must literally equal `include` (line 457) else `Error::InvalidDefinition`. Any other part count is an error (line 477).
- **`name:glob` form**: `name` and `glob` must be non-empty (line 448). Only one glob per `--type-add`, confirmed by the doc ("Only one glob can be added at a time"). To attach multiple globs to a name, repeat the flag.
- **`name:include:othername,...` form**: the third part is split on `,` (line 462). All referenced types must already be defined — checked up front and it fails fast with `InvalidDefinition` if any is missing (lines 465-467). This means **order matters**: the included types must be defined earlier (defaults are always loaded first via `add_defaults`, so referencing built-ins like `cpp,py,md` works). Each referenced type's globs are copied into the new type (lines 468-474).
- **Repeatable**: `Multiple \flag{type-add} flags can be provided.` Each occurrence pushes a `TypeChange::Add` (defs.rs:6895-6898); they are applied in order in `hiargs.rs:1180-1195`. Globs accumulate onto existing globs for that name unless `--type-clear` was used first.
- **Name validation** happens in `add` (types.rs:417-420): `if name == "all" || !name.chars().all(|c| c.is_alphanumeric())` → `Error::InvalidDefinition`. So `all` is a reserved name that cannot be (re)defined, and punctuation in names is rejected.
- **Examples given in the docs** (verbatim from doc_long above):
  - `rg --type-add 'foo:*.foo' -tfoo PATTERN`
  - `--type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md'`
  - `--type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'`

Order-of-application note: all `--type-add`/`--type-clear`/`-t`/`-T` occurrences are collected into one ordered `type_changes` vector (each flag's `update` pushes a `TypeChange`), then replayed in that order in `hiargs::types` (hiargs.rs:1177-1197): `Clear → builder.clear`, `Add → builder.add_def`, `Select → builder.select`, `Negate → builder.negate`. So a `--type-clear foo` must precede the `--type-add 'foo:...'` that redefines it.

---

## 3. Globs / type definitions mapping and the built-in list

- A type maps to **one or more globs**. In `default_types.rs` each entry is `(&[names], &[globs])` — the value is `pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])]` (line 12). The first element is a list of names (aliases) and the second a list of globs. `add_defaults` (types.rs:481-492) iterates every name × every glob so aliases each get the full glob set.
- The `Glob` doc (types.rs:96-99): `There may be more than one glob for a particular file type.`
- **File**: `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. Its header comment (lines 1-10) says the list is the defaults ripgrep ships with, kept sorted lexicographically, and that you extend it per-invocation with `--type-add`.
- **Count**: 202 definition tuples (lines like `(&[...], &[...])`), yielding **206 distinct selectable type names** once aliases are expanded (e.g. `bat`/`batch`, `md`/`markdown`, `py`/`python`, `ts`/`typescript`, `cs`/`csharp`).
- Representative name → glob mappings (all from default_types.rs):
  - `ada` → `*.adb`, `*.ads` (line 13)
  - `agda` → `*.agda`, `*.lagda` (line 14)
  - `c` → `*.[chH]`, `*.[chH].in`, `*.cats` (line 36)
  - `cpp` → `*.[ChH]`, `*.cc`, `*.[ch]pp`, `*.[ch]xx`, `*.hh`, `*.inl`, `*.[ChH].in`, `*.cc.in`, `*.[ch]pp.in`, `*.[ch]xx.in`, `*.hh.in` (lines 49-52)
  - `go` → `*.go` (line 92)
  - `html` → `*.htm`, `*.html`, `*.ejs` (line 107)
  - `js` → `*.js`, `*.jsx`, `*.vue`, `*.cjs`, `*.mjs` (line 114)
  - `json` → `*.json`, `composer.lock`, `*.sarif` (line 115)
  - `markdown` / `md` → (aliases, line 166)
  - `py` / `python` → `*.py`, `*.pyi` (line 210)
  - `rust` → `*.rs` (line 232)
  - `toml` → `*.toml`, `Cargo.lock` (line 288)
  - `ts` / `typescript` → `*.ts`, `*.tsx`, `*.cts`, `*.mts` (line 289)
  - `yaml` → `*.yaml`, `*.yml` (line 316)

Globs are matched against the file **name only**, not the full path, and are built with `literal_separator(true)` (types.rs:271-283, 337-346). Type filtering does **not apply to directories** (types.rs:266-270: returns `Match::None` when `is_dir`).

---

## 4. Behavior details

- **Can `-t` and `-T` be combined? Yes.** Selections and negations are stored together in one ordered vector (`Vec<Selection<()>>`, types.rs:307). Test `test_type_not` (defs.rs:7059-7063) exercises `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` together.
- **Can they be repeated to select multiple types? Yes.** Both docs say "Multiple flags may be provided." Tests confirm `-trust -tpython` → two selects (defs.rs:6830-6831) and `-Trust -Tpython` → two negates (defs.rs:7053-7054). Short forms can be glued: `-trust` means `-t rust` (defs.rs:6827).
- **`--type-list` output format** (main.rs:329-347): for each definition (from `types().definitions()`, which sorts definitions by name and sorts each type's globs — types.rs:364-375), it writes `name`, then the literal `": "`, then the type's globs joined by `", "`, then a newline. So each line is exactly `name: glob, glob, ...`. Exit code is `1` if zero types were printed, else `0` (main.rs:347). This reflects any `--type-add`/`--type-clear` in effect (docs, and the builder is fully populated before listing).
- **`--type-clear`** removes the named type entirely from the builder's map: `self.types.remove(name)` (types.rs:406-410). Globs can still be re-added after it in the same invocation.
- **Precedence / negation semantics** (`Types::matched`, types.rs:255-300):
  - Whitelisted if the file matches a **selected** type; ignored if it matches a **negated** type.
  - `has_selected` = true if at least one non-negated selection exists (types.rs:324). If at least one type is selected and the path matches nothing, the path is **ignored** (types.rs:295-297, and the None-filename branch at 275-277). If nothing is selected (only negations), a non-match returns `Match::None` (line 298).
  - **Highest-precedence match is the last matching glob**: `matches.last()` (types.rs:284-285). So when a file matches both a selected and a negated type, whichever glob was added later (i.e. whichever selection appears later on the command line) wins. This is how `-T` can override `-t` — order on the command line determines the outcome. Test `matchnot4` (types.rs:557): `select rust`, `negate foo` (`foo:*.{rs,foo}`), path `main.rs` → **not matched** (negation wins because `foo` was added after `rust`). Conversely `match7`/`matchnot3` (types.rs:548,556): `select foo`, `negate rust`, `main.foo` matches (foo only) but `main.rs` is excluded.
  - Type filtering has **lower precedence than `-g/--glob` and ignore-file rules** (stated in `--type` doc_long: "this flag has lower precedence than both the glob flag and any rules found in ignore files").

---

## 5. Type-name matching vs globs, and the `all` special type

- A **type name** is an exact key lookup in a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` (types.rs:306, 330-336). Selecting/negating an unknown name yields `Error::UnrecognizedFileType(name)` at build time (types.rs:332-334). Names are the alias strings from `default_types.rs` (e.g. both `md` and `markdown`). Type names must be alphanumeric-only (Unicode letters/numbers) — enforced when adding (types.rs:418) and stated in the `--type-add` doc.
- **Globs** are matched only against the file's base name via a compiled `GlobSet` (types.rs:271-283).
- **The special `all` type**:
  - `select("all")` selects every currently-defined type (types.rs:381-390); `negate("all")` negates every type (types.rs:395-404). Documented as "whitelist" mode for `--type=all` and "blacklist" mode for `--type-not=all` in the flag docs.
  - `all` is **reserved**: `add`/`add_def` reject `name == "all"` with `Error::InvalidDefinition` (types.rs:418), so you cannot define or clear a real type literally named `all`.

### Library-level examples (types.rs module doc, lines 12-84)
These runnable doctests illustrate the same behavior for a user guide:
- Select `rust` → `foo.rs` is whitelist, `foo.c` is ignore (lines 22-26).
- Negate `c` → `foo.rs` is none, `foo.c` is ignore (lines 40-44).
- `builder.add("foo", "*.foo")` and `builder.add_def("bar:*.bar")`, select only `foo` → `x.foo` whitelist, `x.bar` ignored (lines 57-67).
- `builder.add_def("bar:include:foo,cpp")`, select `bar` → both `x.foo` and `y.cpp` whitelist (lines 77-83).

### Key file:line references
- Flag defs: `crates/core/flags/defs.rs` — Type 6765-6811, TypeAdd 6841-6900, TypeClear 6928-6961, TypeNot 6990-7033, TypeList 7070-7097; registration list at 136-141.
- `TypeChange` application: `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs:1177-1197`.
- Matching engine: `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` — `matched` 261-300, `select` 381-390, `negate` 395-404, `clear` 406-410, `add` 417-431, `add_def` 442-479, `add_defaults` 482-492.
- Built-in types: `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs:12` (`DEFAULT_TYPES`).
- `--type-list` renderer: `crates/core/main.rs:328-348`.

{"file_path":"<path>","content":"# Filtering by File Type in ripgrep

When you grep text for a living, you rarely want to search *everything* under a directory — you want the Python, or everything except the JSON. ripgrep ships knowing about file types, so instead of hand-writing globs you can name a type and let it do the matching. This guide covers the four flags that drive that system: `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## `--type` / `-t`: search only a type

`-t rust` limits the search to files matching the `rust` type. As the help puts it: "Only search files matching TYPE." A type is just a named set of globs — `rust` means `*.rs`, `py` means `*.py` and `*.pyi`, `js` means `*.js`, `*.jsx`, `*.vue`, `*.cjs`, `*.mjs`, and so on.

You can repeat the flag to widen the net. To search both Rust and Python:

```
rg -t rust -t python foo
```

The short form can be glued to its value, so `-trust` is the same as `-t rust`.

There's a special value, `all`. `--type=all` behaves as if you'd passed `--type` for every type ripgrep knows (including any custom ones you've defined). That puts ripgrep in "whitelist" mode: it searches only files it recognizes via a type definition, and skips anything it can't classify.

One precedence note that matters in practice: `--type` has *lower* precedence than the `--glob` flag and than any rules in ignore files. A `.gitignore` rule or an explicit `-g` still wins over your type selection.

## `--type-not` / `-T`: exclude a type

`-T` is the inverse: "Do not search files matching TYPE." Use it to carve noise out of a search:

```
rg -T json -T lock config
```

Like `-t`, it repeats to exclude several types, and it accepts `all`. `--type-not=all` is "blacklist" mode: ripgrep searches only files it does *not* recognize.

You can freely combine `-t` and `-T` in one command. When a file matches both a selected and an excluded type, **the last matching rule on the command line wins** — order decides the outcome. So `-t rust -T foo`, where a custom `foo` type also covers `*.rs`, excludes `main.rs`, because the negation came later. Keep that in mind when a file could fall under two types.

## `--type-add`: define or extend a type

Type definitions aren't fixed. `--type-add` adds a glob to a type — creating the type if it doesn't exist. There are two forms.

The first is `name:glob`:

```
rg --type-add 'foo:*.foo' -tfoo PATTERN
```

Only one glob per flag — to give a type several globs, repeat `--type-add`. New globs are *added* to whatever the type already had, so extending a built-in type is additive, not a replacement.

The second form pulls in existing types with an `include` directive: `name:include:type1,type2,...`. To make a `src` type covering C++, Python, and Markdown:

```
rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc PATTERN
```

The types you reference must already be defined. The built-ins always load first, so referencing `cpp,py,md` works; but if you're referencing your own custom types, define them earlier on the line. You can mix the two forms — add includes, then bolt on extra globs:

```
rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
```

Two constraints worth remembering. Type names must be Unicode letters or numbers only — no punctuation. And **settings don't persist**: `--type-add` applies only to the invocation it's on. To make custom types permanent, put the flags in a ripgrep configuration file (see the `CONFIGURATION FILES` section of the manual) so every run picks them up.

A companion flag, `--type-clear`, wipes the globs for a named type so you can redefine it from scratch. Because rules apply left to right, a `--type-clear foo` must come *before* the `--type-add 'foo:...'` that rebuilds it.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

When you can't remember whether it's `md` or `markdown` (it's both — many types have aliases), ask:

```
rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line as `name: glob, glob, ...` — the name, a colon, then a comma-separated list of its globs. ripgrep ships with roughly 200 built-in types. Crucially, `--type-list` reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` you pass alongside it, so it's the way to confirm a custom definition came out the way you intended:

```
rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-list
```

## A few things to know

- Type globs match against the **file name only**, not the full path, and type filtering never applies to directories.
- Selecting or excluding a name ripgrep doesn't know is an error, not a silent no-op — `--type-list` is your check.
- `all` is reserved: you can select or exclude it, but you can't define a type called `all`.
